What Japan's rising land prices really tell us about the property market
article:
Japan's latest land price data confirms something those of us in the property market have been seeing for some time now. Land prices are rising again, and the recovery is getting broader.

The latest government survey showed nationwide land prices increasing for a fifth consecutive year, with residential and commercial land both appreciating, and particularly strong gains in the major metropolitan areas.

For a country where falling property values shaped investment decisions for decades, that's a meaningful shift.

But the national number hides more than it reveals.

Japan is not one property market. It comprises dozens of them. What moves a residential building in central Tokyo has almost nothing to do with what moves a hotel in Nagoya or a house in a regional city.

Higher costs and the appeal of older condos

In Tokyo, one of the clearest pressures is simply the cost and scarcity of creating new supply in desirable locations.

Well-located land is limited and construction materials, labor and development costs have all risen sharply.

That combination makes it more expensive to build something new, and it raises the value of existing buildings that are structurally sound and well located.

It is part of why we have spent so many years acquiring older condos and renovating them rather than starting from scratch.

New-build condos in central Tokyo tend to be small — developers size units down to hit affordable price points, given how expensive land and construction have become.

That leaves a gap for buyers who want more space than a new building can offer at a comparable price.

Older condos, many of them originally built with more generous floor plans, fill that gap naturally.

Renovated to reflect what today's buyers actually want — more bathrooms and toilets, for instance — they can be just as compelling as new construction, often at a better price for the space.

How tourism and the weak yen are influencing demand

International visitors have added another layer of demand. According to the Japan National Tourism Organization , Japan welcomed a record 42.68 million international visitors in 2025, up 15.8% from the year before.

That momentum carried into 2026 — July alone brought 3.44 million arrivals , the highest figure ever recorded for that month.

The effect can be seen most clearly in Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto, where hotels, restaurants and retail now compete directly with residential and commercial users for the same square footage.

In some tourism-heavy markets, the impact on land values has been striking; the latest survey showed particularly strong appreciation in destinations that benefit most from inbound demand.

There is also a less obvious link between tourism and investment. Most international buyers' first exposure to Japanese real estate is simply spending time here — the trains, the safety, the quality of construction, the restaurants and the neighborhoods.

Only later does that familiarity turn into an interest in owning something: a residence, an investment property, or a broader allocation to Japan.

The weak yen has made that conversation an easier one to have. Convert a Tokyo property’s value into Singapore dollars or US dollars and it can look inexpensive next to other major global cities.

But currency is only one part of the case, and it is the part most likely to change. Exchange rates move constantly. A building's location, tenant base and physical condition do not.

That is why, when we look at a property, we spend far more time on the neighborhood and the building than on any macro narrative.

Who wants to live there? How good is the transportation? Is rental demand durable, and how much competing supply could realistically get built nearby? Can the property itself be improved?

Those questions, not the macro numbers, are what decide whether an asset holds up over time.

Closer look at Japan's major property markets

National averages can also be misleading in the other direction — they understate what is happening in the strongest markets.

The 2026 government land survey found that prices in the Tokyo and Osaka metropolitan areas rose considerably faster than the national average.

Tokyo has the underlying fundamentals on its side: a steady inflow of population, a vast employment base, deep housing demand and transportation infrastructure most cities can only aim for.

Osaka is building its own momentum, with substantial investment flowing in.

Kyoto has a different character altogether — global tourism demand running into supply that is unusually constrained by geography and history.

Beyond these three, conditions vary enormously by region.

We have made a bet on that kind of local distinction ourselves. LogProstyle built its business primarily in Greater Tokyo, but this September we completed the acquisition of I-Flatz , a condo sales, renovation and leasing company focusing on Osaka and Kyoto in the Kansai region.

The deal gives us a platform to bring the business model we have proven over the past 20 years in Greater Tokyo to Kansai, Japan's second-largest economic region after Kanto — adapted to how business actually works there, not just copied from Tokyo.

Consumer preferences are different there. So is the available housing stock, tourism patterns, and what you can and cannot build. Real estate investment that ignores those differences does not tend to work out.

What comes next for property investors

Rates are moving too. Japan is stepping away from the extraordinarily loose monetary policy that defined the past few decades.

The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, the highest it's been in 31 years.

Borrowing costs now matter more in every acquisition decision we make.

Still, it is worth keeping in perspective that mortgage rates for buyers remain very low by global standards, even after this normalisation, and our own average cost of debt at LogProstyle is still under 3% — low next to what borrowers face in most other developed markets.

If you are an international investor — and I hear this most often from people looking at Japan out of Singapore — the useful move is to get specific, fast.

A national land-price index tells you which way the wind is blowing. It will not tell you whether a given building, on a given street, with a given tenant base, is actually a good investment.

That is a different question, and it has to be answered property by property.

Five straight years of nationwide increases tell us the recovery has real breadth, not just a few hot spots carrying the average.

What comes next is harder: investors will have to tell markets apart from each other, city by city, and sometimes street by street.

Japan's major cities still have limited supply, international demand and a lot of ageing buildings worth a second look.

Those forces are real. But the opportunities that last will keep coming from the same place they always have — understanding why people actually want to live, visit and invest somewhere.

Yasuyuki Nozawa is representative director, president and CEO of LogProstyle , a Tokyo-headquartered, New York-listed real estate platform spanning condo renovation and resale, residential development, investor-oriented property operations, ryokan hotel operations and restaurant brands.

title: SGX Next 50: 3 Stocks Quietly Buying Back Shares
article:
Share buybacks
on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) are having a record year.
In the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), 80 primary-listed companies bought back S$2.38 billion of their shares on the open market.
That figure has already surpassed the S$2.23 billion recorded for all of 2025, which was previously the highest figure in SGX’s 10-year tracking history.
Naturally, the
big market names
drove most of the volume.
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74),
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4), and
United Overseas Bank Ltd
(SGX: U11) accounted for 72% of the overall total.
Three members of the iEdge Singapore Next 50 Index have been buying too.
Food Empire Holdings Limited
(SGX: F03),
Raffles Medical Group Ltd
(SGX: BSL), and
UltraGreen.ai Limited
(SGX: ULG) spent a combined S$27.1 million on 16.9 million shares.
Food Empire spent almost twice as much as the other two combined.

The size of a buyback only tells you so much.
As a dividend investor, you also want to know where the money comes from.
Free cash flow is the engine that keeps both dividend payouts and share buyback programmes running sustainably over time.
Can Raffles Medical keep buying back shares while its profit falls?
On paper, Raffles Medical Group (RMG) had a soft first half of 2026 (1H2026).
Revenue fell 6.7% year on year (YoY) to S$353.2 million, while profit attributable to shareholders slid 9.6% YoY to S$29 million as finance income dropped 52.3%.
Cash flow moved the other way.
The healthcare operator generated S$61.3 million in free cash flow, representing a 17.9% year-on-year increase.
The business also repaid S$51.1 million in bank borrowings during the half.
As at 30 June 2026, the group held S$262.3 million in cash with no bank debt on its balance sheet.
Next to those numbers, RMG’s S$4.8 million of buybacks over 9M26 looks modest, with no on-market buybacks in September.
Don’t be put off by the missing interim dividend.
RMG has paid one core dividend a year since FY2021.
Its final dividend for FY2025 rose to S$0.030 per share, up from S$0.025 a year earlier.

3 Dividend Stocks I Will Buy Now With S$10,000
What is UltraGreen.ai funding its buybacks with?
UltraGreen.ai Limited, the newest listing among the trio, debuted on the SGX Mainboard in December 2025.
The company specialises in producing indocyanine green (ICG), a medical dye used widely in fluorescence-guided surgery.
In 1H2026, revenue rose 24.3% YoY to US$87.2 million, driven by a 29.6% increase in ICG sales.
Net profit attributable to owners grew at an even faster pace, leaping 53% YoY to US$39.2 million.
Free cash flow slipped 5% YoY to US$23.8 million.
As at 30 June 2026, the group held US$65.5 million in cash alongside US$132.1 million in short-term treasury investments.
Its only borrowings are US$5 million in lease liabilities, leaving the company with a robust net cash position.
Over 9M2026, UltraGreen.ai bought back 3.82 million shares worth the equivalent of S$4.4 million while also declaring an interim dividend of US$0.01 per share.
Management remains confident in its outlook and expects FY2026 revenue of US$175 million to US$185 million, with the second half expected to be stronger than the first.
Related articles:
Beyond Blue Chips: 3 SGX Stocks Quietly Buying Back Their Own Shares
iEdge Singapore Next 50: Top 3 Stocks With Extra Dividends (Sept 2026)
Is Food Empire buying back more than its cash flow covers?
You may know Food Empire through MacCoffee, its 3-in-1 instant coffee brand.
For 1H2026, revenue rose 15% YoY to US$315.1 million, with positive growth across all six operating segments.
Attributable net profit came in at US$35.4 million, turning around from a net loss of US$1.5 million a year earlier.
That previous loss was largely caused by a one-off, non-cash fair value adjustment of US$32.6 million; adjusting for that item, underlying net profit was up 13.6% YoY.
Cash flow is where it gets tricky.
Capital expenditure more than doubled to US$30.1 million during the period, dragging free cash flow down from a positive US$20.5 million a year ago into a negative US$4.1 million.
Fortunately, the company retains a comfortable buffer.
As at 30 June 2026, it held US$151.3 million in cash against US$100.7 million in total debt, giving it a net cash balance of US$50.7 million.
Negative free cash flow has not stopped the buybacks.
Food Empire was the biggest buyer of the three, spending S$17.9 million on buybacks over 9M2026 – with 38% of it in September alone.
Management also raised its interim dividend payout to S$0.04 per share, up from S$0.03 a year ago.
The spending on new plants isn’t over yet.
Food Empire’s coffee-mix plant in Khorgos, Kazakhstan, began contributing from 2H2026.
The spray-dried coffee expansion in India is due by end-2027, with a freeze-dried facility in Vietnam to follow in 2028.

title: Inflation-Proofing Your Kids: Why Cash Savings Might Be a Risk in 2026
article:
I remember it very clearly.
One of the first things I did when my daughter was born was to open a children’s savings account (and a Child Development Account, or CDA) for her.
The plan my husband and I had was to regularly put in a small amount every month, as well as
ang bao
money she would get from her first-month celebration or at future birthdays and even during the Chinese New Year season.
When our second and third children came along, we did the same for them.
The assumption was that this saving habit would build up to a nice, sizeable amount that they could eventually use for university tuition, their first home, or whatever big milestone lay ahead.
Seeing those account balances grow brought a great deal of comfort.
Unlike stock prices, cash feels solid and safe.
You deposit S$1,000, and six months later, it’s still S$1,000.
And maybe
that
is the problem.
Over time, while cash preserves the nominal digit in a bank book, it quietly destroys what that money can actually buy.
With university fees and daily living costs climbing across Singapore, holding too much cash for a long period presents a silent, ongoing challenge for our children’s future.
Why Cash Savings May Not Be as Safe as They Seem
Inflation acts like a silent tax on savings.
When prices rise, the purchasing power of every dollar shrinks.
To put this in perspective: at a steady 3% annual inflation rate, an expense costing S$10,000 today will shoot up to roughly S$18,061 in 20 years.
That means the S$10,000 you have in the bank today will not buy as much as it does now.
Singapore’s
core inflation
is projected to average 1.5% to 2.5% in 2026.
Meanwhile, basic kids’ savings accounts or standard bank deposits often yield base rates well below that mark.
Real return is what remains after subtracting inflation from your interest rate.
If your money earns a 1% base interest rate while inflation averages 3%, your real return is negative 2% each year – meaning your savings are steadily losing real-world value.
Unlike short-term adult savings, money set aside for a child often sits untouched for 10, 15, or even 20 years.
Over such long horizons, even tiny gaps between interest rates and inflation compound into massive losses in purchasing power.
The Real Cost of Raising and Educating a Child
As Prime Minister Lawrence Wong highlighted at the recent National Day Rally, the costs of raising and educating a child continue to weigh heavily on parents, prompting the government to step in with enhanced financial packages and reduced preschool fees.
For instance, under the newly announced
SG Child Support Package
, every Singaporean child will receive nearly S$70,000 in total direct financial support from birth to age 17 – including cash gifts, annual child credits, and post-secondary education top-ups.
While government support provides a welcome boost, the long-term price tag of major milestones remains significant.
University tuition and specialised enrichment programmes historically experience inflation rates that outpace general headline inflation.
Beyond tuition, many parents also hope to help their children with down payments for their first home or postgraduate studies.
Saving a fixed lump sum today without accounting for inflation leaves a shortfall decades down the road.
Rather than assume today’s costs will hold, map out when your child will need the funds and adjust expected expenses upward for inflation.
Why Investing Could Be a Better Long-Term Strategy
To see how much difference investing can make over time, consider a hypothetical S$10,000 saved for 20 years.

While returns are never guaranteed, reinvesting dividends and market gains historically helps build real purchasing power over multi-decade periods.
Broad-market exchange-traded funds (ETFs) offer an accessible starting point by providing instant exposure to hundreds of global companies.
For local dividend income and stability, established Singapore
blue chips
like
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) or defensive real estate investment trusts (REITs) like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, generate steady cash flows that can be automatically reinvested to accelerate growth.
Of course, time helps cushion volatility, but it does not eliminate risk entirely.
Stock markets go through down cycles, and prices fluctuate.
Investing for a child’s future requires accepting this short-term volatility in exchange for potential inflation-beating long-term growth.

How Parents Can Build Their Children’s Wealth Consistently
Building long-term wealth for your children does not require a massive lump sum upfront.
Here is how parents can build that foundation over time:
Start with small, regular contributions:
Putting even a modest
S$200 a month
into a low-cost ETF builds serious compounding momentum over 15 to 20 years.
Reinvest dividends and distributions:
Automatically reinvesting every payout buys more units along the way, quietly multiplying your portfolio’s long-term engine.
Review the portfolio as your child grows:
When your child nears major milestones around age 16 or 17, gradually shift those volatile growth holdings into safer, liquid cash assets to protect what you’ve built.
At the same time, we need to steer clear of a few common mistakes.
While leaving 100% of their money in cash guarantees a slow loss of buying power over time, jumping to the other extreme by chasing speculative, high-risk punts is equally dangerous.
Avoid investing without a clear horizon – putting money you’ll need in two years into equities leaves you exposed if the market takes a temporary dip.
Lastly, don’t miss the chance to
talk to your kids about money
along the way.
Teaching them how saving, interest, and compounding work in the real world ensures they inherit financial wisdom alongside the nest egg you’ve built for them.
Get Smart: Protect Their Future Purchasing Power
At the end of the day, cash isn’t the enemy.
It remains essential for emergency buffers, everyday expenses, and short-term peace of mind.
But holding a child’s entire long-term reserve in a standard bank account for 15 or 20 years quietly exposes their future to serious inflation risk.
The secret lies in matching every dollar to its timeline – keeping near-term funds in safe, liquid accounts while letting long-term money grow in a diversified investment portfolio.
By giving every dollar a clear job and a realistic time horizon, we can ensure the money we save for our children today actually retains its real buying power when they need it tomorrow.

title: Singapore’s MAS unexpectedly holds policy, lowers inflation view
article:
Singapore’s central bank unexpectedly left monetary policy unchanged as it expects both the global energy crunch and the artificial-intelligence boom to ease up next year.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which uses the exchange rate as its main policy tool rather than interest rates, kept the slope, width and centre of its policy band unchanged, it said in a statement on Wednesday. It’s the first pause after consecutive rounds of tightening in its April and July meetings.

Only three of 20 economists surveyed by Bloomberg News predicted the decision, with the majority expecting the MAS to increase the slope of the policy band. A majority of respondents also expected the central bank to retain a hawkish bias.

The Singapore dollar slipped 0.1% to 1.28 per US dollar after the surprise decision.

“The back-to-back tightening in April and July are still working its way through the system hence the central bank sees no need to add further to the tightening at this point,” said Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group. “But this does not mean the end of the tightening cycle. If upside inflation risks eventuate next year, then the MAS may tighten further.”

The MAS narrowed its forecast for core inflation to 1.5%-2% for this year, from the previous projection of up to 2.5% at its July meeting. Headline inflation should come in at around 2%, it said.

Both gauges are seen to average 1.5%-2.5% next year, with import costs and supply disruptions to energy and food ebbing. Domestic price pressures should stay subdued, also aided by government subsidies to health and education.

Core inflation should “remain slightly elevated in the immediate quarters ahead,” before it’s projected to “ease discernibly” from mid-2027, the central bank said. In July, it had said it expected inflation next year to “moderate discernibly.”

The MAS — the first central bank in Asia to tighten monetary policy after the outbreak of the Iran war earlier this year — may be taking its time to assess how persistent price pressures are after core inflation climbed to a two-year high of 2.2% in August.

See also: Singapore power rates to fall from record after fuel price drop

Public transport fares will be hiked in December, following an increase to electricity and gas fees last quarter. The re-escalation of fighting in Iran, as well as the weather disruptions from El Niño, threaten to fan food and fuel costs further.

The current policy stance can “lean against the anticipated near-term rise in imported inflation, ensuring the gradual easing of inflationary pressures in 2027,” the central bank said. “MAS is well-positioned to respond effectively to any risk to medium-term price stability and will continue to closely monitor economic developments.”

GDP Growth

That’s happening against the backdrop of robust economic activity and demand in Singapore. Gross domestic product expanded 5.4% in the third quarter, according to advance data released by the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry on Wednesday.

While it slowed compared to the revised 6.2% print in the second quarter, it beat the 5.1% median forecast in a Bloomberg survey. It’s also at the upper end of the MAS’ forecast of 4.5%-5.5% growth for this year.

The global AI boom continued to drive Singapore’s factory activity, services and exports. Some of the top performing sectors were construction, which saw growth accelerate to 8.8%, as well as wholesale and retail trade, transport and storage.

“The Singapore economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, and moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten,” the MAS said. - Bloomberg

title: Fed’s Lisa Cook puts off White House hearing over Trump’s allegations
article:
(Oct 14) : Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook says she will be unable to attend a Nov. 5 hearing at the White House that’s part of a new investigation into mortgage fraud allegations by President Donald Trump.

Cook will be “executing her official duties as governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe” then, her lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said in a letter to the White House on Tuesday.

Lowell wrote that a hearing would have to take place after the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting so that Cook had enough time to prepare and to accommodate other scheduling conflicts.

In a memo last week, Trump announced that a committee would investigate his claims that Cook committed mortgage fraud. He said she’d have to appear at the White House for a hearing to defend herself. The investigation is the latest escalation in Trump’s ongoing effort to oust Cook from her role at the Fed.

Trump first attempted to fire Cook last year, the first such action by a president in the Fed’s history. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court held that Trump failed to provide Cook with enough notice and an opportunity to defend herself before attempting to remove her, but didn’t spell out what that procedure should look like.

The justices left it to the White House to create a process that would survive another round of legal wrangling.

See also: Asia stocks to gain on signal for fewer Fed hikes

Cook has denied the mortgage fraud allegations, casting them as a pretext to remove her from office and allow the president to reshape the Fed more to his liking.

Lowell, in his letter, expressed skepticism about “the objectivity and fitness of the committee for its assigned purpose.”

“For example, one of the committee’s three members,” Trump’s chief economic adviser, Kevin Hassett, “already has publicly insinuated that the president has “cause” to fire Governor Cook,” he said.

See also: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows

title: Asia stocks to gain on signal for fewer Fed hikes
article:
(Oct 14) : Asian stocks looked set for broad gains on Wednesday after US equities recovered from session lows on signals that the Federal Reserve may not need to raise interest rates aggressively next year.

Equity-index futures for Japan and South Korea advanced, while those for Australia edged lower. The S&P 500 closed little changed and Treasuries rallied after New York Fed President John Williams said he continues to see one more rate hike as appropriate this year, but currently sees no need for further tightening in 2027. The dollar fell.

A selloff in chipmakers also eased, with a sector gauge trimming its loss to 0.2%. Microsoft Corp. rose to a record, while the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.3%.

US oil edged higher after Brent crude steadied following three sessions of gains. Saudi Arabia intercepted more missiles and drones launched by Yemen’s Houthis on Tuesday, with fighting against the Iran-backed group showing few signs of easing.

Williams’ comments came ahead of a key US inflation report that may help determine how quickly the Fed moves again. Higher gasoline costs probably pushed headline inflation higher in September, while an easing in underlying price pressures may give policymakers more room to wait before tightening further.

“Confirmation that underlying inflation moderated last month would allow the Fed to approach the timing of its next rate hike with patience rather than urgency,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

See also: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows

As the US earnings season got underway, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Citigroup Inc. and Wells Fargo & Co. set a fresh record in the third quarter for how much they earned from lending, with customers continuing to borrow even as interest rates increased.

At Goldman Sachs Group Inc., equity traders beat expectations, while fixed-income and rates trading fell well short of Wall Street estimates.

Still, stock traders appear largely sanguine. The S&P 500 Index hasn’t suffered a 1% decline in 53 trading sessions through Tuesday, marking the longest such stretch since January 2020, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

See also: Stocks bounce from lows on Williams’ rate remarks

“Such a long streak of tranquility is certainly surprising, given all of the renewed fears swirling around rising interest rates, a spike in bond yields and elevated oil prices the past few months,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments LLC.

In Asia, Indian stocks will be in focus after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said she’s open to discussions about a transaction tax on share trading as the country seeks to boost capital inflows. The Nifty 50 extended gains as she spoke Tuesday, closing 1.6% higher for its biggest advance in more than two months.

Elsewhere, the yen was little changed in early trading after people familiar with the matter said Bank of Japan officials are leaning against a rare back-to-back interest-rate increase this month, while keeping open the possibility of another move as soon as December.

In the US, Williams’ comments pulled Treasury yields lower, with the two-year yield almost erasing a three-basis-point rise. He expects inflation to slow “quite a bit” toward the Fed’s 2% target next year as the effects of tariffs and an energy shock fade, reducing the need for further tightening.

“I haven’t changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike,” Williams said Tuesday in an interview with Bloomberg News at the New York Fed. “I don’t think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more” after that.

title: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows
article:
(Oct 14) : Oil rose as a flare-up in attacks in the Middle East increased uncertainty over a recovery in energy flows from the Persian Gulf.

West Texas Intermediate advanced toward US$95 a barrel, after edging higher in the previous session, while Brent declined to close below US$106. The US said it assisted in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude through the Strait of Hormuz, even as an escalation of Iranian attacks on tankers in the waterway threatens the recent rebound in Gulf supply to near prewar levels.

Elsewhere in the region, Saudi Arabia intercepted more missiles and drones launched by Yemen’s Houthis, as fighting with the Iran-backed militant group showed few signs of subsiding. The headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco in the east of the kingdom was hit in the latest attacks.

Brent has surged more than 70% this year as the US-Iran war roils energy markets. Risks have intensified as Iran-backed Houthis attacked Riyadh’s main airport last week and Saudi-backed forces launched a campaign to reclaim rebel-held territory in Yemen. Tanker strikes in Hormuz have also prompted more supertankers to turn away from the Persian Gulf.

“While the day-to-day headlines constantly move, the overarching picture in the Persian Gulf has been little changed throughout the past three months,” said Pavel Molchanov, an analyst at Raymond James. Tanker companies are becoming more adept at moving crude between vessels at sea to keep exports flowing, while reducing exposure to Iranian attacks, he said.

title: Stocks bounce from lows on Williams’ rate remarks
article:
(Oct 14) : Stocks bounced from session lows as speculation the Federal Reserve won’t be forced to raise rates aggressively offset lingering worries about elevated oil prices and the outlook for artificial intelligence.

While the S&P 500 closed little changed, most of its firms rose after Fed Bank of New York President John Williams said he still sees one more hike as appropriate this year, but currently doesn’t believe it will be necessary to lift rates again in 2027. Bond yields fell. A selloff in chipmakers waned, also helping sentiment. Microsoft Corp. rose to a record.

“I haven’t changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike,” Williams told Bloomberg News. “I don’t think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more” after that.

His remarks came ahead of a key reading on consumer prices. Higher gasoline costs probably led to quicker overall inflation in September even as underlying price pressures moderated.

“Confirmation that underlying inflation moderated last month would allow the Fed to approach the timing of its next rate hike with patience rather than urgency,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the surge in long-term Treasury yields is helping to curb demand in rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and automobiles, doing some of the work of tighter monetary policy.

See also: Asian stocks to fall after US chipmaker sellof

“When yields go up, is that going to impact interest-sensitive sectors like housing and autos and other things? Yeah, of course it is,” Waller said at Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum in New Delhi. While that isn’t the Fed’s intention, higher yields are “doing a little bit of the work,” he said.

As the earnings season got underway, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Citigroup Inc. and Wells Fargo & Co. set a fresh record in the third quarter for how much they earned from lending, with customers continuing to borrow even as interest rates increased.

As Wall Street’s fixed-income desks struggled in the third quarter, their rivals in equities seized a rare opening to outshine their market brethren.

See also: Oil holds advance as expanding Middle East war threatens supply

Equities divisions at five of the largest US banks are on track to deliver more than US$66 billion of revenue in the first nine months of the year, roughly US$3 billion higher than what’s expected from units handling bonds, currencies and commodities. Part of that was driven by prime brokerage operations catering to hedge funds and other big stock investors.

title: Apple unveils US$299 HomeView Hub as part of new smart home push
article:
(Oct 14): Apple Inc introduced a new device called the HomeView, a US$299 display that serves as the centrepiece of its push to challenge Amazon.com Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google in the smart home market.

The product, which will be available on Nov 13, relies mainly on hands-free voice commands and uses facial recognition to provide a personalised software experience for each member of the household. There are no physical buttons on the HomeView, though its 7-inch touch screen has a grid of apps that will instantly feel familiar to iPhone and iPad users.

Apple is framing the HomeView as the ideal showcase for its Siri AI assistant: Using a built-in camera, the device can instantly recognise up to six different users and give personalised responses for each individual, whether they’re using it as a cooking companion, videoconferencing with a relative or just listening to music through its speakers.

To help rapidly expand its presence in the smart home, the company is partnering with LG Electronics Inc and Schneider Electric SE to release a lineup of “Apple Home Collection” accessories, such as indoor and outdoor cameras, a video doorbell, thermostats, and door locks. Apple codeveloped the hardware, which will begin shipping in December at prices ranging from US$199 to US$399.

Alongside the HomeView, the company also announced an upgraded Apple TV 4K set-top box — now with built-in microphones and an easier-to-find remote control — and the HomePod mini 2 speaker, which comes in a new batch of colors and has lighting animations that match the album art of whatever song is being played.

See also: ASML’s guidance key to instill confidence in fragile chip trade

Both of those products have increased in cost compared with their predecessors, part of a broader wave of price hikes fuelled by the shortage of memory chips and other components. The US$149 HomePod mini 2 will be available on Oct 30, and the US$299 Apple TV 4K will follow on Nov 13. That compares with a starting price of US$199 for the previous TV box and US$129 for the HomePod mini. Both new devices can be pre-ordered on Tuesday, along with the HomeView.

Apple is offering two different styles of its first-ever smart display. The one most consumers will purchase is a tabletop design with an aluminum base and an adjustable stainless steel hinge that lets users freely tilt the display on counters or nightstands.

See also: China’s CXMT claims memory advances ahead of Samsung, Hynix

The company will also sell another version of the HomeView, at the same US$299 price, that’s designed to be placed on the wall. The tabletop version is powered with a standard USB-C cable, while the wall-mounted product will support a range of different options, including power over Ethernet, or PoE, which could ease installation.

The 7-inch screen is square in shape — a design Apple chose to help distinguish it from the wider displays of TVs and monitors — and automatically adjusts its brightness and colour balance to match the HomeView’s environment. The screen has a maximum brightness of 500 nits and can dial all the way down to 0.3 nits, the lowest level of any display the company has ever manufactured. That will prevent it from being a distraction at night on a bedside table.

The software experience is identical across both models, with the ability to show various clock-like “faces” whenever HomeView is idle. There’s a Photos Face, an Apple Watch-like Modular Face with four customisable widgets, a Snoopy Face with playful animations of the Peanuts comic character, and several more traditional clock faces.

Some faces, like one called Flow, can shift colours and patterns based on movement detected in front of the device’s 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Alternatively, users can choose to have HomeView serve as a smart home command centre, showing controls for door locks, lights and other gadgets, or provide a live feed of connected video cameras.

Whenever HomeView recognises household members, it will display their personalised home screen of applications, widgets and calendar appointments. Siri AI, Apple’s recently upgraded digital assistant, is able to leverage its database of knowledge about each specific user when answering requests or sending messages. The HomeView always relies on a nearby iPhone for personal context; that data isn’t stored directly on the device.

Apple has adopted several privacy safeguards to prevent one family member from seeing another’s private data. If a known user leaves the camera’s view, HomeView will revert to its default shared household mode in just a few seconds. Additionally, each person’s iPhone must be on the same WiFi network as the HomeView in order for Siri AI to tap into personal data. The phone also must have recently been unlocked.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Apple said it wants HomeView to be useful when someone first wakes up in the morning — without requiring them to authenticate — so this “recent” window stretches several hours, and the company may further adjust it based on customer feedback.

If HomeView can’t identify who’s standing in front of it, the device will show a generic screen with less extensive smart home controls: Guests can adjust a thermostat or toggle lights, but they’re unable to control smart locks or access a security camera’s video history, for example.

HomeView includes versions of the company’s popular apps, like Apple TV, Music, Calendar, Podcasts, Safari and more, but there’s no App Store on the device. According to the company, third-party audio and video software that supports Apple’s CarPlay architecture will appear on the smart display just as they would on a vehicle dashboard. This will let services like Spotify work on the HomeView even without a conventional app marketplace.

By bringing an iPhone close to the HomeView, you can “hand off” music playback, FaceTime video calls and Safari web browsing sessions to the new device. Apple has also created a special cooking mode that converts recipes into step-by-step guides optimised for the screen. Whenever a cooking time is mentioned, you can simply tap it to create a timer for the specified length.

In a hands-on demonstration, the HomeView’s speakers were loud and clear — though the bass wasn’t as impactful as on the full-sized HomePod speaker, which costs US$349. The new device is smaller than many people might expect, and the HomeView’s display is shorter than an iPhone 17 Pro Max. Apple’s demonstrations of Siri worked smoothly when asking general knowledge questions and in specific scenarios like asking about appointments and controlling lights.

But the biggest challenge for the HomeView is whether it will prove reliable and work consistently as the central element in complex smart home environments. As a blend of the iPad, Apple Watch and HomePod, the appeal and functionality is there: Apple just needs to prove that the dependability will be just as impressive.

The various devices that Apple developed with LG and Schneider Electric include:

These products, known as the Apple Home Collection, will start shipping in December. Availability will be limited to Apple’s own stores before expanding to other retailers in the coming months. All of the gadgets can be set up using an iPhone without requiring any extra apps or separate accounts, and they integrate seamlessly into Apple’s ecosystem.

The latest Apple TV 4K now has microphones built into the set-top box itself. That allows for hands-free Siri AI voice commands from your couch, even when the remote is out of reach. On the TV screen, Apple’s assistant replies with text overlays rather than speaking aloud. But it will be useful for asking to play a TV episode or show that a friend recommended when the actual name escapes you.

The aluminium remote’s design is unchanged, but it can now emit a sound when lost in the cushions to make it easier to find. Users can even activate precision finding on an iPhone to pinpoint the remote’s exact location if needed.

Apple is giving the new box one other exclusive feature: You can group up to four HomePods for immersive front and rear surround sound. Previously, they could only serve as front speakers. But now you can combine pairs of the second-generation HomePod and the HomePod mini 2 — or four of the same speaker — for a much more engrossing audio experience.

Even with its newfound functionality, the Apple TV 4K’s increasingly steep price might dissuade all but the most hardcore home theater enthusiasts from upgrading.

Apple’s small wired speaker, now US$20 more expensive, looks identical to its predecessor save for fresh colours. The new choices include green, pink and blue, along with more neutral white and midnight options. The chipset inside has been upgraded to the S10 for faster processing, and a new “Sound Glow” feature makes the touch surface on top illuminate in different hues. It can show the same color palette as album artwork or match ambient soundscapes like rain or forest sounds.

And for recent Macs with WiFi 6E, the HomePod mini 2 can be used as a default external speaker with low-latency audio when playing games or joining video calls.

Siri AI will eventually come to the device, but not until a “later” software update, according to Apple.

The company is unveiling this wave of smart home hardware just days before the arrival of its long-awaited iPhone Duo foldable phone. Consumers can place orders for that device on Oct 16, a week before it hits stores.

Apple is also planning to unveil a touch-screen MacBook Pro and an updated iPad mini — both with sharper OLED screens — at the end of this month, Bloomberg News has reported. It’s all part of a record-setting surge of new products under chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month.
